extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and practitioners of political philosophy, policymakers and advocates concerned with civil liberties
extracted.subtask_description: A compact set of principles governing when society (collectively or through government) may legitimately exercise power over individuals — chiefly the harm principle, its exceptions, and associated liberties (thought, expression, conduct, association).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm Principle (sole end of legitimate interference)
rubrics_metrics.description: "That the sole end for which mankind are warranted, individually or collectively, in interfering with the liberty of action of any of their number, is self-protection."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill's central rule: the only legitimate purpose for exercising power over a member of a civilized community against his will is to prevent harm to others. The individual's own good, whether physical or moral, is not sufficient ground for compulsion — at most for remonstrance, persuasion, or disapprobation. To justify compulsion, conduct must be "calculated to produce evil to some one else." (Examples/notes: distinguishes self-regarding acts from other-regarding ones; repetition throughout the essay.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual sovereignty over body and mind
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the part which merely concerns himself, his independence is, of right, absolute. Over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill locates the proper sphere of liberty in self-regarding actions: bodily and mental autonomy should not be overridden by society or law. This is a normative baseline for judging interventions: if an action affects only the agent, it should not be subject to coercion. (Implication: evaluate policies by whether they intrude on this inward domain.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of thought and discussion (absolute conscience and opinion)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It comprises, first, the inward domain of consciousness; demanding liberty of conscience, in the most comprehensive sense; liberty of thought and feeling; absolute freedom of opinion and sentiment on all subjects..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom to hold and form opinions is absolute in Mill's account. Speech and publication are closely linked but discussed separately because they affect others; nevertheless, freedom of expression is "practically inseparable" from liberty of thought. (Anti-pattern: suppressing beliefs because of majority sentiment or 'moral sense'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of expression (practically inseparable from thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The liberty of expressing and publishing opinions may seem to fall under a different principle... but, being almost of as much importance as the liberty of thought itself... is practically inseparable from it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although expression concerns others, Mill argues it must nearly always be protected because of its role in truth-seeking and personal development. Restrictions must still be tested against the harm principle. (Guidance: treat limits on expression with the same strictness as limits on thought.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of tastes, pursuits, and life-plans
rubrics_metrics.description: "Secondly, the principle requires liberty of tastes and pursuits; of framing the plan of our life to suit our own character; of doing as we like... so long as what we do does not harm [others]."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals should be free to pursue unconventional, foolish, or unpopular ways of living provided they do not harm others. Social disapproval alone does not justify coercion. (Evaluation criterion: does the conduct impede others' rights or efforts?)

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of association / combination
rubrics_metrics.description: "Thirdly... the liberty, within the same limits, of combination among individuals; freedom to unite, for any purpose not involving harm to others..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People of full age, not forced or deceived, may freely associate and organize provided their purpose does not harm others. Collective activities are permissible so long as they remain within the harm-principle bounds. (Test: purpose and effects on non-consenting third parties.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limited to mature, capable persons
rubrics_metrics.description: "This doctrine is meant to apply only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties. We are not speaking of children... those who are still in a state to require being taken care of by others must be protected against their own actions..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill excludes children and persons lacking mature faculties from full liberty protections; the law may legitimately exercise paternalistic control over them. Similarly, in 'backward' societies despotism may be permissible to achieve improvement. (Application: age and capacity tests determine applicability.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive duties that society may compel
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are also many positive acts for the benefit of others, which he may rightfully be compelled to perform; such as to give evidence in a court of justice; to bear his fair share in the common defence..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all compelled obligations are forbidden: society may enforce certain duties that directly secure others' interests or the public good. Mill lists examples (testimony, conscription, rescue/protection of the defenseless). The distinction: compelling to prevent harm or to discharge clear communal obligations is legitimate. (Policy relevance: identify duties tied to protecting others' interests.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability for inaction (omissions) — caution required
rubrics_metrics.description: "A person may cause evil to others not only by his actions but by his inaction... The latter case... requires a much more cautious exercise of compulsion than the former."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While omissions can ground responsibility, Mill treats enforcing responsibility for inaction as the exception and to be applied only in clear and grave cases. Enforcement should weigh evidentiary and practical difficulties. (Guidance: prefer voluntary moral responsibility unless harm is substantial and avoidable.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions where compulsion should not be enforced
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are also many good reasons for not holding him to the responsibility; either because... he is on the whole likely to act better, when left to his own discretion... or because the attempt to exercise control would produce other evils, greater than those which it would prevent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when conduct affects others, compulsion can be inappropriate if (1) leaving discretion yields better outcomes, or (2) intervention produces greater harms. Policymakers must consider second-order effects and weigh utility. (Decision rule: intervene only when net utility favors intervention.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of societal tyranny include moral coercion and prevailing opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: "Protection... against the tyranny of the magistrate is not enough: there needs protection also against the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill emphasizes non-legal social pressures (ostracism, opinion) as powerful and pernicious forms of coercion that can 'penetrate much more deeply' and 'enslave the soul.' Limits on majority influence should include protection from social as well as legal penalties. (Evaluation: assess non-state sanctions and their intrusion into private life.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny of the majority — need for safeguards for minorities
rubrics_metrics.description: "The will of the people... practically means the will of the most numerous or the most active part... the people, consequently, may desire to oppress a part of their number; and precautions are as much needed against this as against any other abuse of power."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic accountability does not eliminate the risk of oppression: majority opinion can impose harms. Institutional and moral safeguards are required to protect minorities. (Policy implication: majority rule must be limited by rights-based principles.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper basis of social rules: reasons not mere preferences or class interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill diagnoses that social rules are often produced by "likings and dislikings" or by class interests and unreasoned preference rather than by reasons. He argues that opinions on conduct should be supported by reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimacy of social norms and legal rules requires rational justification rather than mere popular preference or the interests of an ascendant class. When evaluating whether society should coerce, ask whether reasons (not mere liking) justify making a rule enforceable. (Anti-pattern: enacting laws grounded only in majority taste or class bias.)

rubrics_metrics.name: When external enforcement is unadvisable, rely on conscience (moral self-regulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "When such reasons as these preclude the enforcement of responsibility, the conscience of the agent himself should step into the vacant judgment seat... and protect those interests of others which have no external protection."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill recommends moral education and the cultivation of conscience as the fallback when legal compulsion is unjustified or impracticable. Social policy should aim to foster internal responsibility where external coercion would be harmful or ineffective. (Application: prefer persuasion and moral suasion when feasible.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism permissible for 'barbarians' if justified by improvement and effective results
rubrics_metrics.description: "Despotism is a legitimate mode of government in dealing with barbarians, provided the end be their improvement, and the means justified by actually effecting that end."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill carves a narrow exception to his liberty principle for societies judged incapable of improvement by free institutions: coercive rule may be justified instrumentally. This is a conditional and controversial exception and should be applied only where it demonstrably promotes improvement. (Caveat: historically and morally fraught; requires strict evidentiary standards.)
